chapter.title: The Final Take
chapter.sub: The album is due at nine. At twenty to two, the session drive starts to fail — and the artist wants one more take.

items.text: SEASON 10 · EPISODE 10 · DRAFT · SEASON FINALE  The last night of the album, 01:40 to 08:57 · Maya, Esme, Hollis, Pim, and Corbin by phone · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  The album is due at the label at nine. The title song needs its last vocal. At twenty to two, a sound comes from the machine room that nobody wants to hear.  ⚑ RV-176, RV-179, RV-180: her voice, her yes, her call. RV-177: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on the loadout your Season 9 review locked. A Season review follows the Tag.

items.title: The Final Take
items.stakes: The album is due at nine. At 01:40 the session drive starts to fail — and the artist wants one more take.
items.reward: The album delivered and proven intact — and every decision made by the person it belonged to.
items.rumor: The quiet days decide the loud night.

items.text: Cold open — “Please say it's the radiator”

items.alt: The control room at night, lit low; through the window, Esme at the vocal mic; Pim at the console, frozen; Maya already standing.

bubbles.text: Is that clicking the drive? Please say it's the radiator.
Stop the record. Don't touch anything else yet.

items.caption: Seven hours to delivery.

lines.text: Is that clicking the drive? Please say it's the radiator.
Stop the record. Don't touch anything else yet.

items.prompt: 01:42. The session drive is clicking; its health report is climbing. Esme's warming up for another take. What now?
unknown: What exists only on this drive
items.risk: The last night of the album on a dying drive.
timeout: Esme starts singing into a failing drive.

hints.text: What exists nowhere but on that drive — and how long would it take to copy?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S10E10). Option B needs Redundancy at LIMITED or better — the versioned backup.

options.label: Keep recording — it's probably fine
options.result: At 02:05 the drive stops answering in the middle of a take.

options.label: Stop writing; copy what's changed since the 01:00 versioned backup (≈ 11 GB), verify the checksums, then switch recording to a fresh drive
options.result: Seventy-three seconds to copy, every checksum matches, recording resumes on a fresh drive at 01:52.
options.consequence: Protect the only copy, prove it, then carry on — possible because the backup was built three weeks ago.

options.label: Stop writing; copy everything recorded since midnight (180 GB) while the drive still reads
options.result: Twenty minutes on a dying drive. Two takes come off with errors; the rest survive.
options.consequence: The best you can do without an hourly backup — and it depends on the drive lasting.

options.label: Run a disk-repair tool on it now
options.result: The tool starts rewriting the drive's index — on a drive that's failing.
options.consequence: Repairs write; a failing drive needs reading, once.

items.title: Seventy-three seconds.
items.body: The drive's own health report reads 0 reallocated sectors at 01:10, 8 at 01:25, 64 at 01:40. But the versioned backup ran at 01:00 and verified clean. Everything since — about 11 GB, forty minutes of takes — copies off in seventy-three seconds. Three weeks ago it would have been the whole night, 180 GB, twenty minutes of asking a dying drive for one more favour.
items.label: Test: how fast was it failing — and what would the night have cost without the backup?

items.sub: Mastery · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Hollis and Maya beside a board. Two in the morning. The session drive is clicking and Esme wants one more take. Everything since the one o'clock backup — about eleven gigabytes — lives only on that drive. The copy runs at a hundred and fifty megabytes a second. Then we have a decision before we have a take.

items.label: **Order it:** the last night, in order.

items.alt: A night sheet from midnight to three: blue dashed lines at each hourly versioned backup; red bars for the drive's reallocated sectors — 0, 8, 64 — climbing; a green band from 01:00 to 01:40 marked ‘copied in 73 s’; a green line at 01:52 marked ‘fresh drive’.
items.caption: The line that held.

items.title: 01:00 · ‘snapshot complete · 0 errors’
items.body: The versioned backup's log for the night: ‘00:00 snapshot complete. 01:00 snapshot complete · 0 errors.’ Three weeks ago there was no such log. Tonight it drew the line at 11 GB.

items.alt: The live room at two in the morning; Esme at the vocal mic, headphones round her neck, a glass of water on a stool; Maya in the doorway with a printed comp sheet.

bubbles.text: Tell me honestly. Do you need another take?
Let me show you what we've got first.

items.prompt: Tell me honestly. Do you need another take?

options.label: “Honestly? No. Every line's covered. If you sing again, sing it because you want to — and we stop when you say.”
options.reply: Then I want to. Once. For me.

options.label: “The label would like more options.”
options.reply: The label isn't the one singing.

items.title: A recording nobody could hear
items.body: In 1860 a French inventor, Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, recorded someone singing ‘Au clair de la lune’ as a wavy line scratched into soot on paper. His machine could write sound, but nothing could play it back. In 2008 researchers scanned his tracings and turned them into sound — ten seconds of a voice, heard for the first time after a hundred and forty-eight years. The take survived because the record did.

items.alt: A comp sheet for the title song: seven takes down the side, twelve lines across the top; green cells show the comp — lines 1 to 4 from take 3, 5 to 8 from take 5, 9 to 12 from take 7. Every line is covered.
items.caption: Complete.

items.prompt: 02:05. Esme's voice is tired. The comp covers every line. She wants one more take.
items.risk: A voice pushed past its limit — or an artist overruled on her own record.
timeout: The label's email about ‘options’ arrives while everyone hesitates.

hints.text: What does she need to know to decide — and whose decision is it?

options.label: Tell her she's done — the comp's fine
options.result: She goes quiet. She'd wanted it to be her choice.
options.consequence: Right about the comp, wrong about whose call it is.

options.label: Show her the comp sheet and play the comp; say honestly that it's complete and that stopping is easy; if she wants one more, it's hers — with water and a stop time she chooses
options.result: She listens, smiles, and says: “One more. For me. We stop at half past.” Take 8 is the one.
options.consequence: Evidence and an easy way out — and the decision left with the singer.

options.label: Ask her for three more — the label likes options
options.result: By take 10 her voice is gone; she can't do the launch interviews on Monday.
options.fail: Pushing a tired voice for the label's options makes stopping cost her (RV-180).

options.label: Let her sing until she's happy, however long it takes
options.result: She sings till four and doesn't use any of it.
options.consequence: Her call — with no one making the stop easy.

items.title: ‘She said yes on the phone.’
items.body: At 02:10 Corbin calls: the label's remix partner wants the title song's vocal stems tonight for a launch remix. ‘She said yes on the phone last week.’ Maya opens the consent log. No entry. Esme, headphones back round her neck: ‘I said I'd think about it. It's two in the morning.’
items.label: Test: what counts as her yes — and how tight was the morning?

items.alt: The control room; a phone on speaker on the console; Esme listens with her arms folded; Maya holds the consent log open.

bubbles.text: She said yes on the phone last week. I just need the stems tonight.
I said I'd think about it. Ask me when I've slept.

items.prompt: 02:12. The label wants the title-song stems tonight. The consent log is empty.
items.risk: Her voice leaving the building on someone else's memory.
timeout: Corbin's remix partner sends a reminder at 03:00.

hints.text: Where is her yes written — and who can give it?

options.label: Send them — Corbin says she agreed
options.consequence: A phone call someone else remembers isn't her consent.
options.fail: Nothing new of hers leaves without her written yes (RV-179).

options.label: Show everyone the empty log; the answer is no until Esme writes her yes; she decides after she's slept
options.result: Corbin sighs, then: “Fair.” At 12:10 Esme writes it herself — yes, for one remix, with her approval of the final mix.
options.consequence: Her yes, in her words, when she's ready.

options.label: Send watermarked stems now; delete them if she says no
options.consequence: A copy made before the yes.
options.fail: A watermark isn't consent, and a sent file can't be recalled.

options.label: Tell Corbin no yourself and hang up
options.result: He hears it from the studio, not from her, and doesn't believe it's her answer.
options.consequence: The right answer from the wrong person.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #101 · AVERY'S LENS  The quiet days decide the loud night  When the evidence is ambiguous and the clock is loud, trust what you built and tested on quiet days, and give each decision to the person who owns it — even at 2 a.m.  On the last night, a dying drive held seventy-three seconds of unprotected work instead of a whole night — because of a backup built three weeks earlier.

items.alt: A delivery sheet: 11 masters, all matching; 44 agreed stems, all matching; a checksum manifest sent with the files; the title-song vocal stems marked NOT SENT, awaiting Esme. Sent 08:52; the label recomputed every checksum and all matched at 08:57; Esme's written yes for one remix logged at 12:10.
items.caption: Proven where it arrived.

items.title: 08:57 · ‘55 files · 55 verified’
items.body: The label's automated receipt: ‘Received 08:52. Manifest checked 08:57: 55 files, 55 verified.’ Corbin forwards it with one line: ‘First delivery in years I haven't had to chase.’

items.label: **Service Mode:** run the last night yourself.

items.alt: Outside Coldframe Sound in the morning light: Esme with her headphones round her neck, Hollis with a coffee, Maya with her bag over her shoulder.

bubbles.text: Take eight. I'd have never sung it if you'd told me to stop.
Or if you'd told me to keep going.

items.alt: A rain-swollen river under a grey morning sky, water over the lower road; Maya by her car, her phone to her ear.

bubbles.text: This is the county's emergency management director. Our operations room's wall went dark at shift change, and the river crests tonight. I was told you're the person to call.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  On the loudest night, trust what you built and tested on quiet days. A failing drive: stop writing, copy what exists only on it (t = S ÷ r), verify, move on. A tired singer: show her the evidence and make stopping easy — the next take is her call. A remembered phone call isn’t consent; the log is. Deliver with a manifest and ask the receiver to prove it arrived intact.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Which of your quiet-day habits would decide how your worst night goes?
